extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato, literary scholars, and philosophers
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing Plato on poetry and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Critical exposition of Plato's objections to poetry and the arts and an analysis of features and paradoxes of the Republic (ideal state), including educational, moral, and aesthetic prescriptions. The page is an academic treatment aimed at interpreting and evaluating Plato's positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor profession degrades human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘One man in his life’ cannot ‘play many parts;’ the characters which the actor performs seem to destroy his own character, and to leave nothing which can be truly called himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato regards the actor as the slave of his art, not the master of it; acting undermines personal authenticity and is therefore a degradation of human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic/rhetorical power incompatible with firmness of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Great dramatic or even great rhetorical power is hardly consistent with firmness or strength of mind, and dramatic talent is often incidentally associated with a weak or dissolute character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of dramatic or rhetorical skill may indicate susceptibility to emotional display rather than moral steadiness; evaluate dramatic talent against standards of moral firmness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist/poet as imitator (third-degree removed from truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet or painter is an imitator, and in the third degree removed from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato’s epistemic objection: artistic representation is at best a copy of sensible things, themselves copies of the Forms; thus art is distant from ultimate truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art can ennoble humble subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist may ennoble the bed which he paints by the folds of the drapery, or by the feeling of home which he introduces; painters have imparted such an ideal interest to a blacksmith’s or a carpenter’s shop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defense of art: even when representing particulars, skillful artistic treatment can impart dignity, pathos, and an ideal quality beyond mere likeness (examples: Rembrandt, Turner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Great art embodies something higher than mortal form
rubrics_metrics.description: Had Plato been asked whether the Zeus or Athene of Pheidias was the imitation of an imitation only, would he not have been compelled to admit that something more was to be found in them than in the form of any mortal; and that the rule of proportion to which they conformed was ‘higher far than any geometry or arithmetic could express?’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for greatness in art: conformity to a higher rule of proportion or an embodiment of the divine/ideal beyond mere sensory form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative arts primarily express emotion not reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato objects to the imitative arts that they express the emotional rather than the rational part of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate imitative works by whether they primarily stimulate passion (a potential danger) or promote rational reflection; for Plato this is a damning feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts judged by whether they purge or indulge passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato does not admit Aristotle’s theory, that tragedy or other serious imitations are a purgation of the passions by pity and fear; to him they appear only to afford the opportunity of indulging them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key evaluative question: do artworks cathartically purify emotions (Aristotle) or merely provide means for their indulgence (Plato)? The answer influences whether art is seen as beneficial or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure arts by the good they do
rubrics_metrics.description: He asks only ‘What good have they done?’ and is not satisfied with the reply, that ‘They have given innocent pleasure to mankind.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test for arts in Plato’s critique: their value is determined by concrete moral and educative benefits, not merely by pleasure they afford.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry concerns inferior faculties and particulars of sense
rubrics_metrics.description: He tells us that he rejoices in the banishment of the poets, since he has found by the analysis of the soul that they are concerned with the inferior faculties... the higher faculties have to do with universals, the lower with particulars of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry is criticized for addressing particulars and sensory particulars rather than universal truths; this is a reason to distrust its authority for moral and philosophical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets are not authoritative interpreters or rules of life
rubrics_metrics.description: He saw, too, that the poets were not critics—as he says in the Apology, ‘Any one was a better interpreter of their writings than they were themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat poets as reliable moral guides; their works are open to better interpretation than they themselves provide, so their authority as life-rulers is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets and artists can be purveyors of falsehood and servants of tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The poets are also the representatives of falsehood and feigning... there is another count put into the indictment against them by Plato, that they are the friends of the tyrant, and bask in the sunshine of his patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess literature and art for political complicity: whether they flatter power, spread false ideas, or otherwise aid despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: The vocation of art is to present thought in the form of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The vocation of art is to present thought in the form of feeling, to enlist the feelings on the side of reason, to inspire even for a moment courage or resignation; perhaps to suggest a sense of infinity and eternity in a way which mere language is incapable of attaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive standard for art: it should translate ideas into affective form that supports reason and moral sentiments (courage, resignation, reverence), rather than merely titillating lower passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative art is a compromise between ideal and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: All imitative art is subject to certain limitations, and therefore necessarily partakes of the nature of a compromise. Something of ideal truth is sacrificed for the sake of the representation, and something in the exactness of the representation is sacrificed to the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by how successfully they balance fidelity (exactness) and idealization (truth); the permanent element of art is its ability to idealize and detain passing thought as an intermediate between sense and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s worth varies historically and socially
rubrics_metrics.description: In the infancy of mankind, poetry... is the whole of literature, and the only instrument of intellectual culture; in modern times she is the shadow or echo of her former self, and appears to have a precarious existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poetry in context: its social and historical role changes, so its functions and value must be judged relative to the stage of civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art can corrupt religion and philosophy; it is not inherently equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: Art cannot claim to be on a level with philosophy or religion, and may often corrupt them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art’s relation to religion/philosophy, consider potential corrupting influence; art is not automatically a substitute for religious/philosophical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible ideal poetry: hymn of divine perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: There might be a poetry which would be the hymn of divine perfection... which would find materials in the living present as well as in the romance of the past... which might elicit the simple principles, or, as Plato would have called them, the essential forms, of truth and justice out of the variety of opinion and the complexity of modern society... which should be based not on vain longings or faint imaginings, but on a clear insight into the nature of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive ideal for poets: produce works that renew moral imagination, draw from present life, extract essential truths and justice, preserve the good while leaving the bad unsung, and ground art in clear human insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wholesome imagery in education of youth
rubrics_metrics.description: In the third Book, he insists that youth should be brought up amid wholesome imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational standard: regulate the imagery presented to children to ensure it fosters healthy moral development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique degenerate poetry: demand seriousness and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato protests against the degeneracy of poetry in his own day... against the want of serious purpose in modern fiction, against the unseemliness or extravagance of some of our poets or novelists, against the time-serving of preachers or public writers, against the regardlessness of truth which to the eye of the philosopher seems to characterize the greater part of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literary works for seriousness of purpose, propriety of form, resistance to time-serving flattery, and fidelity to truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should gently harmonize feeling and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The beauty which meets the sense like a breeze and imperceptibly draws the soul, even in childhood, into harmony with the beauty of reason.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic criterion: beauty’s role is to softly orient sensibility toward rational and moral harmony, especially formative in childhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude in marvelous narratives via touches of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The verisimilitude ... the precision with which the soul is mentioned... the passing remarks... add greatly to the probability of the narrative. They are such touches of nature as the art of Defoe might have introduced when he wished to win credibility for marvels and apparitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical writing guideline: include specific, plausible details and human touches to increase credibility in fantastic or marvellous storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtue requires knowledge in addition to habit
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue which is founded on habit is not sufficient to enable a man to choose; he must add to virtue knowledge, if he is to act rightly when placed in new circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical standard: assess moral character by both practiced habit and underlying philosophical knowledge; true choice for the good needs informed understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of will within the walls of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom of the will to refuse the evil and to choose the good is distinctly asserted... The life of man is ‘rounded’ by necessity; there are circumstances prior to birth which affect him (Pol.). But within the walls of necessity there is an open space in which he is his own master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical criterion about human agency: evaluate actions considering both deterministic constraints and genuine spheres of voluntary moral choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulative features of Plato’s ideal State (Spartan elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of his regulations are characteristically Spartan; such as the prohibition of gold and silver, the common meals of the men, the military training of the youth, the gymnastic exercises of the women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the Republic as a political design, consider these prescriptive institutional measures as deliberate moral-political devices modeled on Sparta: economic restrictions, communal dining, militarized youth training, and public physical training for women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens forbidden to trade; soldiers not shopkeepers
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizens of Sparta, like Plato’s, were forbidden to trade—they were to be soldiers and not shopkeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for civic design: restrict commercial activity among full citizens to preserve a martial, civic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure of deformed children and intrusive social welfare rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the best enactments in the Republic... and some of the worst, such as the exposure of deformed children, are borrowed from the practice of Sparta.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral-political critique: Plato’s state includes harsh eugenic-style measures; evaluate such measures for ethical cost despite their purported civic rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage as public institution and state education of women
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage was a public institution: and the women were educated by the State, and sang and danced in public with the men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-policy criterion: regulate family life publicly and include women in state education and public ritual as part of civic formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict regulation of music and poetry for moral ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The new-fangled poet was to be expelled. Hymns to the Gods, which are the only kind of music admitted into the ideal State, were the only kind which was permitted at Sparta.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural policy standard: limit permissible musical and poetic forms to those deemed morally and politically wholesome (e.g., hymns); proscribe subversive or decadent forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage relationships (men with youths) as incentives to bravery
rubrics_metrics.description: The encouragement of friendships between men and youths, or of men with one another, as affording incentives to bravery, is also Spartan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social engineering criterion: cultivate certain interpersonal bonds to foster civic virtues like courage—evaluate such policies for efficacy and ethical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean influence: importance of music and mathematics in education
rubrics_metrics.description: There is yet another thread... the Republic is not only a Dorian State, but a Pythagorean league... The influence ascribed to music... is also a Pythagorean feature; ... the great though secondary importance ascribed to mathematics in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational standard in Plato’s design: include music and mathematics centrally in curricula as formative disciplines for harmony and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradoxes of the Republic as evaluative test (community and rule of philosophers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paradoxes of the Republic... (a) the community of property; (b) of families; (c) the rule of philosophers; (d) the analogy of the individual and the State, which... is carried too far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these paradoxical prescriptions as focal points for critique: test plausibility, moral desirability, and social consequences of communal property/families, philosopher-kings, and analogical reasoning between soul and state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of ideals despite impracticality
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing actually existing in the world at all resembles Plato’s ideal State; nor does he himself imagine that such a State is possible... ideals are none the worse because they cannot be realized in fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-criterion: treat utopian prescriptions as normative guides or patterns that have intellectual and moral value even if not practically realizable; evaluate political thought partly on its idealizing power.
